premise.coldViewerWhyCare: People may mistake chemically and clinically distinct kratom-related opioid-active compounds for interchangeable retail products.
premise.viewerQuestion: How do mitragynine, 7-OH, MGM-15 and corynoxine B differ, and what can we actually say about safety?
premise.earlyPayoff: They differ in plant occurrence, receptor activity, synthetic status and depth of evidence; lab activity is not a safe dose.

sourcePacket.note: No human potency or safety ranking permitted. MGM-15 currently Schedule I federally (2026-10-10).

conceptCandidates.viewerHook: The molecules are related; risk profiles aren't
Do lab assays predict the danger?

beats.narration: Four kratom-related compounds. Not the same drug.
beats.onScreenText: FOUR COMPOUNDS. NOT THE SAME DRUG.
beats.visualPurpose: Show four distinct molecules as cards around one μ-opioid receptor; forbid invented relative potency.
beats.visualAction: At spoken phrase 'same drug', reveal the teaching graphic. Show four distinct molecules as cards around one μ-opioid receptor; forbid invented relative potency.

beats.narration: Mitragynine dominates kratom leaf. Concentrated seven-OH has stronger opioid activity.
beats.onScreenText:
MITRAGYNINE: MAIN LEAF ALKALOID
7-OH: HIGHER OPIOID ACTIVITY

beats.visualAction: At spoken phrase 'seven-OH', reveal the teaching graphic. Leaf-to-concentrate visual; distinguish natural leaf abundance from enhanced products without assigning a conversion ratio.

beats.narration: MGM-fifteen is a synthetic derivative with strong lab binding, and little human safety evidence.
beats.onScreenText:
MGM-15: SYNTHETIC DERIVATIVE
HUMAN SAFETY DATA: LACKING
beats.visualPurpose: Chemical derivative link and lab evidence lens; no numerical potency ranking.

beats.narration: Corynoxine B binds opioid receptors in experiments, but human effects remain unclear.
